title: Package weight normal interval probability
scenario_markdown: A high-speed cereal packaging line fills family-size boxes with net weights that follow a normal distribution with mean $\mu = 500$ grams and standard deviation $\sigma = 8$ grams ($X \sim N(500, 8^2)$). Quality assurance standards accept boxes whose net weight falls between $490$ grams and $510$ grams. What is the probability that a randomly selected box meets this quality specification ($P(490 < X < 510)$)?
assumptions: Continuous normal distribution X ~ N(500, 8^2) in grams
Independent packaging fill trials identically distributed
Standard normal table / cumulative normal distribution applies

approval.delegation_basis: Content backlog Batch 1: Row 3.2 normal distribution expansion

stages.prompt_markdown: What are the standardized standard scores ($Z$-scores) corresponding to the lower and upper specification limits $X_1 = 490\text{ g}$ and $X_2 = 510\text{ g}$?

options.hint_markdown: Standardization requires dividing the difference between each raw bound and the mean by the standard deviation $\sigma = 8$.
The $Z$-score formula is $\frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$, subtracting the mean from the value, so $X_1 < \mu$ produces a negative $Z$-score.
Each interval endpoint must be standardized individually relative to the distribution mean $\mu$.

stages.explanation_markdown: $Z_1 = \frac{X_1 - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{490 - 500}{8} = -1.25$ and $Z_2 = \frac{X_2 - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{510 - 500}{8} = +1.25$. The specification limits lie symmetric at $1.25$ standard deviations below and above the mean.

stages.prompt_markdown: Find the probability that a package weight falls between $490\text{ g}$ and $510\text{ g}$: $P(490 < X < 510) = P(-1.25 < Z < 1.25) = \Phi(1.25) - \Phi(-1.25)$. Enter as a decimal or percentage rounded to four decimal places.
stages.explanation_markdown: Using standard normal tables or software: $\Phi(1.25) \approx 0.89435$ and $\Phi(-1.25) = 1 - \Phi(1.25) \approx 0.10565$. Therefore, $P(-1.25 < Z < 1.25) = 0.89435 - 0.10565 = 0.7887$ (or $78.87\%$, or $2\Phi(1.25) - 1 = 0.7887$). Excel formula: `=NORM.DIST(510, 500, 8, TRUE) - NORM.DIST(490, 500, 8, TRUE)` or `=NORM.S.DIST(1.25, TRUE) - NORM.S.DIST(-1.25, TRUE)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Does the probability $P(490 < X < 510)$ differ from the non-strict interval probability $P(490 \le X \le 510)$?

options.text_markdown: No, they are identical. Because $X$ is a continuous random variable, the probability of any exact single point is zero ($P(X = 490) = 0$ and $P(X = 510) = 0$), so including or excluding boundary endpoints does not change the probability.
Yes, $P(490 \le X \le 510)$ is strictly greater because it includes the probability masses at exactly $490\text{ g}$ and $510\text{ g}$.
options.hint_markdown: For continuous random variables, area under the curve at an exact point of zero width has probability zero ($P(X = c) = 0$).

options.text_markdown: Yes, the values differ unless a discrete continuity correction of $\pm 0.5$ is applied to the bounds.
options.hint_markdown: Continuity corrections are only used when approximating a discrete distribution with a continuous one, not when analyzing an inherently continuous variable like weight.

stages.explanation_markdown: In all continuous probability distributions, probability is defined as the area under the density curve over an interval. Since single points have zero width ($dx = 0$), $P(X = 490) = 0$ and $P(X = 510) = 0$. Consequently, $P(490 < X < 510) = P(490 \le X \le 510) = P(490 \le X < 510) = P(490 < X \le 510)$.
